Do I love this game? Yes. Do I recommend this game? Hell no.

Take Karlach for example. You meet her and she’s just standing there all sexy, talking in that deep voice, and you’re like “okay cool companion,” but NO. It’s not that simple.

You recruit her.
You help her.
You fix her engine like some kind of j*b.

And suddenly it’s not about the quest anymore.

It’s about her.

You start picking dialogue options based on what she’d like. Not what’s smart. Not what’s good. What she would approve of. You start waiting after conversations like she might say something else if you just… stay there.

Then it gets weird.

You notice things.
The way she heart pulses.
The way she licks her lips.
The way she says your name so buttery smooth.

You reload saves. Not because you messed up. But because you want to see her react again. Slightly different. Slightly better. Maybe this time she’ll say something more.

Then it gets worse.

You start thinking about her when you’re not even playing.
Like what she’d be doing right now.
If she’d be a top or bottom.
If she’d look at you like you were more than just a player.

You start imagining conversations that never happened.
Moments that aren’t in the game.
Things she’d say. Things she’d do. Things you’d do to her.

No, it’s fine. It’s normal. Totally normal.

Until it isn’t.

Because now you’re staring at the screen a little too long.
You’re leaning in a little closer.
You’re saying stuff out loud like “yeah… yeah you would.”

And at some point you realize.
You don’t even care about the story anymore.

It’s just her.

Just Karlach.

And the way she moves her body.
And the way her chest bounces as she walks.
And the way you’d absolutely do her in until her infernal engine combusts.

Like if she was real you would probably never pull out.
And honestly? You’d do it again.
No hesitation. No regrets. Just you and Karlach and a bottle of "stuff".

I would describe [b]Baldur’s Gate 3[/b] as “bootleg D&D”.

It’s a “popcorn” game, which is to say it’s fun and good but ultimately artistically insignificant, just barely a step above other popular generic fantasy games, and I’m giving it a thumbs down ONLY because I don’t think it deserves the 720.000 “overwhelmingly positive” score.
(However, I’ll change it into a thumbs up if the score ever dips below it)

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
Locales are good looking and have variety in them, physical and voice acting are on point, music does the job but sprinkles in some banger tracks, and the changes to the original D&D rules are mostly great and well implemented.
Also, it’s offline D&D, so if you ever missed a session or want to see how a build works you can always fire up this game and just do it.

Despite being a series of rigamarole fetch quests, most setpieces are very cool.

Importantly for replayability, even more than multiple classes with multiple abilities granting no end to how you can build your character, is the modding scene, adding just about everything to freshen the game up for a second and third go-around.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
It’s D&D fifth edition.
If you don’t know what that is: You choose how good a character is at something by slotting a certain number of points in six scores that define who you’re playing as.
On top of this you choose a “class” or what kind of things you’d want your character to be centered around, each class providing different mechanics to achieve this, both inside and outside combat, along with different equipment to give you that extra edge to succeed.
There’s a lot of nuance but that’s pretty much it.

[h1]Story[/h1]
You find yourself aboard an alien ship and infected with a brain parasite that threatens to turn you into a monster, so partner up with an unlikely cast of characters in your quest to seek a cure for this shared burden.

A good hook that gives an excuse to be joined by anyone, no matter how good or evil they are, as you need eachother’s expertise to find a solution to this problem.

The story progresses mostly through dialogue, simply walk up to someone to talk and be either given quests or advance them.

The game also features LOTS of side stories and especially questlines for the ones that either want to explore more of this world or to satisfy their inner completionist.

[h1]Downsides[/h1]
An interesting and focused story that could’ve been told in a couple of hours was instead overfilled with generic writing and other filler content stretching it to about a 100 hours where the game keeps bumping into weird pacing, losing momentum, reiterating over already-made points, and sending you off onto yet another wild goose chase when it doesn’t want you to get to the point, again, all of this isn’t necessarily a bad thing depending of the level of writing required for your enjoyment.

In D&D players can say and do anything they want whenever they want and the DM reacts to it.
In BG3 you’re stunted in your roleplay choices, because of course you can’t have a simple system that accounts for every possibility, but even then, I don’t exactly like how most dialogue choices are: Yes, Yes, Snarky Remark, *attack*.
Also, unfortunately outside a few quips almost no companions interact with eachother, only with the situation at hand which makes them feel more like reactionary robots than the alive characters that should’ve been.

From a purely aesthetic aspect I don’t think anyone will argue about how bad the camera system, the overcrowded UI, the million magical effects overlapping, and other constant immersion breaking aspects of it are, although there are community-made mods that thankfully partially fix some of those issues.

It’s very generic.
That itself isn’t a bad thing but if you want anything more than what the term “fantasy game” conjures in your head, this is not it.
A lot of characters are set up to be interesting in the themes they could explore, but then the writing team ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed and makes them say the same generic trite lines over and over again.

It tries to replicate the tabletop RPG feel but fails to capture its spark.
What is the true TTRPGs experience?
True D&D is a social exercise where you hang out with friends and say dumb stuff and you all laugh at the dumb stuff you say with the plot/campaign only there to give a pretext/context and game rules as a safety net to avoid a guy just going "and then I punch him and he dies and we win".
This game is singleplayer at heart while all TTRPGs are to be played with friends.
It has a hard focus on story but without having good writing to justify it, nor trying to capture the insanity and/or silliness that is player agency.

An even better description for it would be “Singleplayer MMO from the 2000s” but with better graphics that’s only related to TTRPGs due to its D&D playrules.
If that’s sounds like your cup of tea, I’d suggest it, even at full price as there’s a lot of content for those who have the right appetite for it.

Baldur’s Gate 3 shines in its writing and characters. The narrative is well-crafted, and the world feels alive thanks to memorable personalities and engaging dialogue. It’s the kind of game I wanted to love, and the story alone almost carries it. However, the experience is held back by fundamental flaws in its combat and design. Flaws that make it hard to recommend wholeheartedly.
[h2] Combat: A Frustrating Power Fantasy [/h2]
I don’t oppose turn-based games by default, but BG3’s combat doesn’t deliver the power fantasy it promises. When facing 20 weak enemies in a single room, I should feel like an unstoppable force, clearing them in seconds, not gambling with accuracy rolls and damage dice for foes that should die to a stiff breeze. The game constantly throws overwhelming numbers at you (unless you save-scum, which shouldn’t be a core “feature”), and it feels like lazy design.
[b] SPOILERS FOR ACT 3 AND SHADOWHEARTS QUESTLINE IN THE BLOCK BELOW! [/b]

[spoiler] The basement in Act 3 during Shadowheart’s questline was the tipping point for me. I had to cheese my way through with a firewall on the stairs just to get past the relentless enemy spam. It’s not challenging; it’s tedious. [/spoiler]
[h2] Design Disconnect: Combat vs. Story [/h2] 
It’s clear the writing and combat design happened completely independent of each other. The game pretends to offer meaningful story choices, but in reality, most paths lead to minor dialogue tweaks or game-over screens. I played as a resist Durge sorcerer, expecting surrendering to the urge to open new narrative branches. Instead, I got a few lines of unique dialogue and some superficial changes. This isn’t Fallout: New Vegas, where choices ripple through the world! It’s a puddle compared to an ocean.
The disconnect extends to the game’s tone. BG3 forces you into a rigid D&D 5e simulation, complete with RNG and spreadsheet math, but it lacks the camaraderie and flexibility of a real tabletop session. As a DM, I know that level 1 goblins would cower or die in a funny, narratively satisfying way, not force the player to slog through every roll.
[h2] Industry Trends and Award Hype [/h2]
[b] Not really about the game, but important if you're considering getting the game because of it's critical acclaim. [/b]
BG3’s near-perfect scores and GOTY wins say more about the industry than the game itself. It’s not that Alan Wake 2 or other nominees are bad. It’s that awards, like movie Oscars, favor grand, cinematic experiences over smaller, tighter designs. BG3’s 96% “Overwhelmingly Positive” Steam rating is misleading (not really, but let me cook): only around a quarter of players have earned the “All’s Well That Ends Well” achievement (finishing the game). 
[h2] The Community and Criticism [/h2]
[b] Once again, not really related to the game, but still interesting imo [/b]
The most frustrating part isn’t the game, it’s the patronizing fanbase in my opinion. Criticizing BG3’s flaws invites vicious backlash. The fact that there’s a dedicated keybind for loading quicksaves speaks volumes: the developers know players are save-scumming to tolerate the combat. Yet, pointing this out gets you labeled as “not getting it” or worse. (This is not exclusive to BG3, just a flaw with CRPGs in general)
I suspect many positive reviews come from players who didn’t finish the game but don’t want to admit it. That may be out of fatigue or fear of being piled on by the community. Or maybe they just played the first act, enjoyed it but never touched the game again, which is probably the best way to experience it.
[h1] Final Verdict: A Flawed Gem [/h1]
Baldur’s Gate 3 is a game I wanted to love, and its story and characters almost make up for its flaws. But the combat is a slog, the choices are shallow, and the design feels disconnected. It’s a game most players haven’t even finished, yet it sits at near-perfect scores. That’s not a testament to BG3’s quality. It’s a sign of how low the bar has fallen.
If you’re here for the story, you’ll find a lot to enjoy. If you want satisfying combat or meaningful choices, you might leave as frustrated as I did.
Not Recommended (after one playthrough as a resist Durge sorcerer, reaching Act 3).

I woke up after 50 hours jumping like a frog on some platforms like a turn-based Mario.

There are no tactics. There's a mnemonization of spells, items, and stats. Instead of thinking about which hill to place your shooter on, you wonder how the Magic Brooch of Ass you're wearing affects your rolls against the Sudden ♥♥♥♥ Spell.

They advertise that you can fight with the environment. Okay, you set something on fire, the enemy burns. It took a staggering 5% of their HP. So, back to the Sudden ♥♥♥♥ Spell stats. The only effective way to play the environment is to push them into a cliff, but the developers designed a loot loss to prevent anyone from playing like that. But if they stuck to "realism," the loot from a burned fireball victim would be unusable too.

The characters are crap. Protagonists and antagonists. Most attack both melee and ranged at the same time, making tactics pointless. They're jumping around like monkeys (a turn-based Mario), making it impossible to create any sort of structured gameplay. Battles are chaotic in the worst sense of the word.

The monkeys jump around like in a zoo, but at the same time, there are strict rules for blocking characters. You can't send your tank to the front because your team is blocking it. And it's set up the way it is because scripted dialogue set you up at the beginning of the battle. So, good luck with a tank at the back. This happens many times; you'd have to trigger conversations with the tank to keep it in the front. But why would you choose someone else as your main character if a tank with low charisma is supposed to talk?

Therefore, to do ANYTHING in this game, you need to have online help open because nothing is intuitive. There are difficult games, very difficult games, but intuitive. Where losing is fun. Here, you have great sessions with Gemini and discussions on how to prevent Gale from dying in the first turn. In BG3, losing is frustrating because you have no control over your initial setup, every enemy has a ranged attack, and everyone can jump like a monkey. It ends with you being surrounded and pelting your team with everything they can: arrows, spells, bottles of various substances.

That's what the Viet Cong did to every commando unit they spotted in the jungle in Vietnam. But those commandos were hiding, and my team of clowns has to engage in open battle. Often after swaggering dialogues.

As for the lesser sins, the inventory menu is clunky. Like something from 2000.
The camping system is tedious. Halfway through a dungeon, you have to return to camp because your spells and special moves have run out. Furthermore, camping is clearly at odds with the main plot, which counts down to a specific event in single days. Your camping days are unrelated to this; the dialogues constantly state you have a few days left until the event, but you've already camped a dozen times.

If you grit your teeth and endure what I've described, the game is beautiful. Maybe you're into D&D stats, then this is the game for you. But I had to tell the truth about the gameplay because it was touted as a game with good tactical combat, which it isn't.
A little light on content, but I wouldn't bother refunding. Not bad for an indie game.

One moment it's a love story about good triumphing over evil, the next it's ambivalence toward participation in a polyamorous orgy with people you met a minute ago. 

I'd be fine with these characters if they had principles, if Gale was really a homosexual, or Shadowheart was really a polyamous homosexual, if Halsin was a homosexual... if Wyll was a homosexual... if Astarion was a homosexual. But Larian wants to please everyone so we're just supposed to forget that literally every male companion I've been nice to and had a friendship with wants to have sex with me because I've chosen not to relent to their advances. And advances they were, which just makes it all the more strange and taints every future encounter with these characters. It's fine if you want to make a game where everyone is homosexual, go for it. But I also reserve the right to not be able to relate to the characters at all, and that's where we're at. 

It's a shame because many of the characters were very promising. Shadowheart is a great love interest. Gale is a charming, almost roguish wizard and very charismatic. Astarion is excellently acted. Wyll is also very likeable. But it's all tainted by this hamfisted sex sim gameplay that adds literally nothing to the game, especially when you realize that they will be and do whatever you want them to be and do if you click the right responses.

Take Cyberpunk2077 as a contrast. I liked Judy way more than Pamam. Yeah. Too bad. Judy told me straight up to get lost. She's a character written with intent, and CDPR didn't care that I liked Judy, they cared about what Judy wanted. That's the way Larian should have handled all of this, but in an effort to please everyone, they made their characters flimsy and ultimately two dementional. It's a real shame because the non-romance characters like the Devil or the Emperor or the Chosen are all superb, proving that Larian could have done this with your closest companions, but instead tainted them with this weird sex stuff that does nothing but distract. Would it have killed the PC if Shadowheart had simply had a bit of sensibility and refused to have a bisexual orgy with total strangers? I guess the takeaway is that everyone you interact with meaningfully in Baldur's Gate is a sex crazed pervert who is down for everything like they've been snorting lines all night. Uggh.

And that's really the biggest problem. The game is epic otherwise, with a lot to do and see, good gameplay, interesting quests, meaningful choices, and some great set piece battles. This game is overrated due to the branding of Baldurs Gate" and its close match to D&D mechanics.

Combat is over 50% of this entire game and it feels bland (dialog is the another 40% and movement is the remaining 10%). 1 Action per turn, no cover system, missing 9/10 times when hit chance is 70%, too many gimicks to try to gain a single extra action one turn that just seem like moving tokens around from one panel to another in some cases, you don't even get this option for every class and not until you're a good clip into the game. As a Wizard you get a ton of spells and cantrips but most are pointless to use, you just gravitate to using the same 1 or 2 all the time. I found myself heavily relying on Magic Missile just to ensure that I was actually landing some hits since you miss like your blind most of the time even at point blank range. Cantrips are a last ditch effort when you have no more spell slots but are very weak and never seem to improve in damage as the game progresses. As a Barbarian you just have the option to hack and slash and you whiff a lot so combat really has minimal choice required. As a barbarian it's walk up to something and keep swinging one (miss). action (critical miss). per (miss). turn (15 dmg). at (miss). a (critical miss). time (critical miss).

Yes, they have a "Karmic Dice" feature to help with your attack rolls but this spills over to checks outside of combat too and swings both ways. The result is you make too many rolls you should fail (20% chance of success) and fail too many rolls you should make (75% chance of success). Fortunately this feature can be disabled.

Several mechanics were stapled on and feel hollow and pointless:
Camp supplies - Types of supplies you use don't matter for effect. Not like you gain extra bonus if using different types of supplies (there's like 20 different items that are "supplies" but there is no point). As long as you have 40 supply vlaue you can recover in full. Not even finished with act 1 and I've got 1200 supplies and I've been full resting after every battle. What's the point of even having them in the game as a requirement to rest? Who is running out of these things?

Alchemy - Everything is so finite you get very few materials to craft anything. And seems like pretty much everything you can craft are things you can find and buy elsewhere. No limited unique super power craftables looks like. A huge missed opportunity here to have an alchemy skill that allows you to identify rare components to use for unique things. I just don't see the point - you collect a bunch of random bibs and bobs and eventually after a lot of gathering you can craft a basic heal potion.... OoooOOOoo not like they're 15 gold at any trader infinitely.

Relationships - Everyone seems super sex depraved. You can bone anyone in camp with a few dialog selections seems like. You have this whole "party member approves/disapproves" to build some liking between characters but it just seems the only end goal is to bone like we're playing Leisure Suit Larry.

Leveling - Leveling is a joke. While you have a TON of options at initial character creation, you don't really get much choice at each level (the few level ups that there are. 30 hours in and just about level 5). You don't get stat points to add in. It just sort of automatically raises various stats and you get maybe 1 or 2 choices on your level up. You get a new spell slot so you can pick which one from a static selection that you saw last level up. Or some small perk choice. There's really not a lot you can pick and you don't really know what you're getting as a choice on the level up ahead of time. It's not like you're getting stat points and a perk that you can count on each time to develop your character. It's like maybe you get to chose another cantrip or spell. Maybe you can swap a spell out..etc. Just very bland, no choice of progression. If you want to multi-class it's a bit tedious and puts you at a serious disadvantage because you'll be getting level 1 stuff for that other class rather then whatever the higher level stuff you would be getting for your class...etc.  

There's a lot more issues with this game that I won't even go into detail here (loot, camera, save scumming, critical success/failure, mind-worm skill tree...etc) that I think people overlook with rose tinted goggles of the Baldurs Gate series or being a D&D fan. While the graphics are good, the game is pretty well programmed. Story seems decent - though a little ostentatious with some of the side stories of characters. But... the combat is pretty lame. Yes, maybe it's very close to D&D and when you're dealing with pen and paper that may be fine but in a computer game it feels pretty limited and dull. Compared to other titles that are tactical combat RPG style such as a Divinity 2 or Wasteland 3, this combat feels like a massive step backwards for the genre. I don't care that I can stack crates and jump on them mid-battle when I can't even take cover behind one. I would say people should try either of those 2 games over BG3 if they haven't played them yet.

If you're huge fan of D&D or Baldurs Gate for the sake of the name "Baldurs Gate". You'll probably love this game. But if you're coming from playing something like Divinity 2 hoping for something even better - this isn't it. Definitely do your research and watch videos specifically showing the combat in this game and if it's something you're going to enjoy for over 100 hours. Because that is the vast majority of what you'll be doing in this game.

While playing any of the Infinity/Aurora engine games, did you ever caught yourself thinking: 

- Damn, wish this game had platforming! 
- Maybe you would like to spend hours opening barrels and crates to find no loot? 
- How about spending a LOT of time in inventory management, due to small and generic icons, and a LOT of crappy loot?
- Do you want a really clunky UI, that not only doesn't improve on the genre games that preceded this one, but it also makes some things worse?
- You think that highlighting interactable items is too easy, and you want to pixel hunt for items?


If you answer yes to any of the questions, maybe this game is for you...

On a more serious note, this is one of those times that I wish I could leave a neutral review, but Steam doesn't have the option. THE GAME ISN'T BAD, but it doesn't feel like a Baldur's Gate game. Heck, sometimes it doesn't even feel like a Forgotten Realms game. The are a lot of generic places, places that doesn't feel like their lore accurate counterparts, etc...IWD for example got a lot of the ambiance right, and more than 20 years later, BG3 failed to stand on it's predecessors shoulders.


There are also other problems, like some minor bugs, but I find baffling that more than 2 and a half years after release, Larian still manages to introduce new, major bugs with new patches, like with the most current one. Other downsides if I'm being nitpicky: No LVL 20 (the cap is at 12), a party of only four characters, lack of nuance with party relationships, very low variety of armor/weapons, mechanics info (like crit range or calculating base dmg+elemental dmg from weapons is missing), some staple items, like the Bag of Holding and the Holy Avenger are completely absent and the loading screen drives me nuts, loading to 100% and then staying at 100% for a long time, to actually load (the game is on a nvme SSD, so I don't think this is a me problem).

As a last complaint, after seeing the longevity that NWN1 and 2 got by having amazing toolkits, you'd think Larian would give us something comparable, maybe even better after two decades, but, no...There's nothing.


On a brighter side, the game looks good, most of the voice acting is decent to really good (and there's a LOT of voiced lines), The music is good when it is present, some of the small tidbits and sidequests are very well written and the game is long (that can be a plus or a minus...) and very replayable. 

With all that said, I'd say I've played 3/4 of the game, and it keeps growing on me. I might change the review to positive after I end my first run.

I understand why a lot of people love Baldur’s Gate 3. The writing, voice acting, world reactivity, companion interactions, and freedom of choice are impressive. There is clearly a massive amount of work in this game.

That said, I do not enjoy playing it.

The game feels painfully slow. Movement feels like power walking everywhere, combat encounters take way too long, and the pacing constantly drags. I like turn-based games and JRPGs, so the issue is not simply that it is turn-based. The issue is that this feels more like a slow tabletop rules simulator than a smooth video game.

The dice rolls are also constantly in your face. Everything feels like a roll: dialogue, combat, perception, traps, attacks, checks, saving throws, and more. I understand that this is based on Dungeons & Dragons, but as a video game experience, it makes too many moments feel like RNG rather than satisfying player skill. In JRPGs, RNG exists in the background. Here, the game keeps shoving it directly in front of you.

The gear and stat systems are also not explained clearly enough. It is often hard to tell whether one weapon or armor piece is actually better than another because the bonuses, conditions, and mechanics are not intuitive. The game gives you a lot of options, but not enough clarity.

For hardcore D&D fans or players who love slow, tactical CRPGs, this may be a masterpiece. For me, it feels clunky, overcomplicated, slow, and frustrating. I respect the ambition, but (well I realize I am in the minority here,) I do not think it is fun to actually play.

EDIT: Steam currently shows that I have only played this game for around three hours, but that is not accurate. I usually play offline, and Steam does not appear to be counting all of that time correctly. I have put at least 20+ hours into the game because I genuinely tried to give it a fair chance and understand why so many people love it. This review is not based on a quick first impression.

After 232 hours, here is my honest take.

The maps feel small and confined compared to true open-world RPGs like Skyrim or Fallout. Too many invisible walls masquerading as 'strategic terrain.'
There is no real RPG depth. The branching narrative is reactive, sure — but the underlying systems like economy, crafting and faction reputation are basically non-existent.
The dialogue system feels dated, possibly as a nod to Baldur's Gate 1 & 2. Respect the heritage, but someone should have cut 40% of the banter.
The D&D mechanics are faithful to a fault — low hit rates, binary spells and constant save-scumming. This isn't hardcore difficulty, it's just friction.

No clear feedback when actions are blocked in restricted zones. The UI tells you WHAT is blocked but never WHY.

In 2026, with modern AI tools, a solo developer could vibe-code a more polished experience. Just kidding of course but this game deserved better! :(

Not recommended — unless you are 40+ and grew up with Baldur's Gate 1 & 2.

I bought this game because of the massive hype around it, and unfortunately I can’t say I enjoyed it at all.

I was sold on the idea that you can “do whatever you want,” but in practice the game feels extremely restrictive. There were multiple situations where I wanted to do very simple, logical things, like assassinating someone or throwing a sleeping body off a nearby ledge, and the game just outright wouldn’t allow it. Often for no logical reason. Enemies can magically lock doors against you, yet casually run through them themselves. It creates a very caged, artificial feeling.

The flow of the game also feels unnatural. Most meaningful character interactions are forced in camp, marked by giant exclamation points, which completely kills immersion. The same goes for the romance system. Romance is constantly pushed into conversations where it doesn’t belong, often feeling awkward or outright uncomfortable. In my case, most of my camp disliked me, yet immediately after an argument, Gale suddenly acted romantically during what I thought was just a magic lesson. It felt disconnected, forced, and poorly handled.

Dialogue was another disappointment. Even after carefully going through dialogue options, the responses I actually wanted to say often just weren’t there. The game frequently boiled down to: run to NPC, fight, run to another NPC, fight, rest, then awkwardly walk around camp triggering forced interactions. None of it felt natural or immersive.

Graphically, the game is fine, decent, but nothing impressive. Voice acting is inconsistent: some actors do a great job, others really don’t. Overall, nothing stood out enough to make up for the gameplay and design issues.

In my opinion, this game was massively overhyped and ended up being a huge disappointment. I genuinely regret spending $50 on it, especially after saving up for something I thought I would love. Maybe with heavy modding my experience could have been better, but I mod games I already enjoy, not games I’m trying to fix.

A Legendary Franchise Reduced to Shock Value

Let’s be honest: this game is obsessed with sex to a point that feels embarrassing.

Instead of delivering a mature, lore-driven Dungeons & Dragons epic, it constantly drags the player through intrusive sexual tension, unsolicited advances, and dialogue trees that feel engineered to funnel toward sexual outcomes. You can barely interact with companions without conversations bending toward flirtation or outright propositions. It doesn’t feel natural. It feels compulsive.

And when one of the first defining choices in character creation is genital size, that tells you exactly where the priorities were. In a universe built on decades of rich lore, layered politics, divine conflict, philosophical depth, and complex moral choices, this is what they decided to emphasize? It’s juvenile. It’s unnecessary. It cheapens what should feel epic.

The problem isn’t that sexuality exists. The problem is how intrusive and persistent it is. Dialogues corner you. Emotional beats derail into awkward intimacy. Instead of earning connection through storytelling, the game repeatedly defaults to sexual provocation as if that’s the most compelling form of character writing available.

What makes it worse is the generational disconnect.

I started my Dungeons & Dragons journey at 12 years old with Baldur’s Gate I. That game sparked imagination, strategy, moral dilemmas, and a lifelong appreciation for RPGs. Now my own son is 12 — the same age I was when I fell in love with this universe — and I would genuinely feel uncomfortable introducing him to this as his entry point into role-playing games.

Not because fantasy should be sanitized. But because this feels excessive and unfocused. It feels like shock value over substance. Instead of welcoming a new generation into a vast and intelligent fantasy world, the game risks pushing them away with its constant emphasis on genitals and sexual encounters.

And that’s the real wasted potential. This could have been the bridge between generations of players. Instead, it feels like it slammed the door shut.

To be clear: the technical achievement is undeniable. The combat is deep and satisfying. The production quality is extraordinary. The voice acting and cinematic presentation are top-tier. There are moments of brilliance throughout.

Which only makes it more frustrating.

The talent was there. The budget was there. The lore was there.

Restraint wasn’t.

I enjoy a wide variety of videogames, but there's something about CRPGs that will always be special to me. I still remember unwrapping my copy of STAR WARS Knights of the Old Republic II: The Sith Lords, installing it on my dad's old Windows XP box computer (yes, the grey one with a monitor as big as your head), and being transported into a new world of stories and gameplay. It probably ran at a crisp 15-20 frames per second and crashed constantly, but I didn't care. I was immersed in my character, forced to make choices that would alter the fate of party members I had painstakingly nurtured relationships with. 

Much, much further down the line in life, I become engrossed in Divinity: Original Sin II, a Kickstarted game from a relatively small indie studio. It consumed my every waking thought until the credits finally rolled. I of course enjoy many other CRPGs, but something about DOS 2 really gave me a taste of the obsession and immersion I had felt when I was younger. However, I wasn't sure I would experience that same feeling again any time soon.

When Baldur's Gate 3 launched out of early access and into full release, I took off a whole week and a half from my job to stay at home and experience it uninterrupted. It was the best PTO I've ever spent. I remember listening to Alfira's song in the Emerald Grove for the first time, a moment I could have easily missed depending on my dialogue options, and I recall being struck by how truly special this game was. I can't fault any other studios for not having the same level of production value as Larian, but the studio has a unique talent for writing character that really make you care so much about them, feel connected to them, relate to their struggles and empathize with them, motion captured cutscenes or no. 

After 120 hours of gameplay, I watched the credits roll. Unlike many other I've seen online, I couldn't bring myself to dive right back into the game. I needed a break. However, I have returned several times and completed many other playthroughs (though I still have not completed a Dark Urge playthrough, something I am currently working on). In fact, I completed Honor mode in 2024, and am only a handful of achievements away from 100%, something I'd never set out to do for any videogame I have played before. 

I also have to praise Larian for all the years they spent improving and expanding the game from 2023-2025 (for free, I might add).

Baldur's Gate 3 became a gateway for me: I found myself engrossed in D&D actual plays, learning tabletop systems, and even running some games of my own. Honestly, in that way, you could say this game changed my life, as TTRPGs and collaborative storytelling has become a large part of my life. 

I know this is a very long, rambling, poorly formatted review from off the top of my head, but if I had to sum up: The game is good, I think everyone should try it at least once.

And Thank You Larian, for creating a game that made me feel so in touch with my inner child again, and opening a new doorway for so many new fans to the genre.

After nearly 90 hours embedded in the Forgotten Realms, it’s clear that Baldur’s Gate 3 isn’t just a faithful adaptation of Dungeons & Dragons 5e—it is a high-water mark for the entire RPG genre. Larian Studios has built a digital sandbox that somehow manages to feel deeply personal, incredibly chaotic, and meticulously structured all at once.

If you are looking for a game that respects your intelligence, rewards your curiosity, and consequences your lapses in judgment, this is it.

Key Pillars of the Experience
Unparalleled Tactical Freedom: The combat engine is a brilliant translation of tabletop mechanics. Position, verticality, and environmental manipulation aren't just gimmicks; they are survival tools. Whether you’re setting up a perfect ambush from the rafters, triggering a massive chain reaction with grease and fire, or simply shoving an elite boss off a cliff to their demise, the game constantly says "yes" to your tactical ingenuity.

A Living, Reactive Narrative: The writing and voice acting are phenomenal, but the true triumph is the reactivity. Your choices—from major faction alliances down to minor dialogue shrugs—ripple across acts. The companions feel less like scripted digital followers and more like a volatile, deeply human crew with their own agendas, moral thresholds, and trauma to unpack.

Meticulous Map Design: Every square inch of the world feels deliberate. There is zero filler content. You’ll set out to resolve a main questline only to find yourself deep in an underground cavern three hours later, unraveling a completely separate, fully voiced narrative arc because you decided to look behind a hidden wall.

The 89-Hour Perspective
At this milestone, the scale of the game is still staggering. Even when you think you’ve mastered the systems, the narrative shifts or a new environment forces you to rethink your entire approach. It handles high-stakes political intrigue, cosmic horror, and intimate character moments with equal grace.

It runs beautifully on high-end hardware, rendering the dark, gritty corners of the Underdark and the sprawling urban vistas with stunning detail. The audio design—especially the soaring orchestral score and crisp positioning—keeps you completely locked into the atmosphere.

Final Thoughts
Baldur’s Gate 3 is a rare achievement. It demands your time, but it pays you back in pure quality, emergent storytelling, and unforgettable tactical victories. Whether you're a veteran DM or completely new to turn-based strategy, this is an absolute mandatory play.

I went into Baldur's Gate 3 expecting a really good RPG. I did not expect it to completely ruin my standards for what reactive storytelling in games should look like.

This is one of the few games where it genuinely feels like the developers anticipated human behavior instead of just funneling you down content lanes. Every time I thought, “there’s no way the game accounts for this,” it did. Not just with a throwaway line either, but with actual consequences, alternate paths, companion reactions, or some completely unhinged chain reaction that somehow still held together narratively.

What makes BG3 special isn’t just the scale, though the scale is absurd. It’s the density. The world feels hand-touched everywhere. Small choices matter. Weird choices matter. Failed rolls matter. Sometimes your greatest moments come from catastrophically bad decisions and desperately improvising your way out of them.

The companions are probably the best overall cast I’ve seen in an RPG in years because they actually feel like people instead of party archetypes. They’re messy, selfish, loyal, insecure, manipulative, brave, traumatized, funny. Over time the camp starts feeling less like a mechanic and more like a dysfunctional traveling family held together by stress, violence, and mutual bad judgment.

Combat also deserves a ton of credit because it embraces creativity instead of punishing it. The game constantly rewards experimentation. Shove enemies off cliffs. Stack barrels like a lunatic. Turn yourself into a cloud of gas. Weaponize gravity, fire, grease, furniture, or bad ideas in general. It captures the spirit of tabletop RPGs better than almost any adaptation I’ve played because it allows for chaos without collapsing.

And somehow beneath all the spectacle, it still has heart. There’s a real sincerity to the writing. Moments of genuine grief, kindness, fear, and friendship land because the game earns them over dozens of hours.

It’s also gloriously confident in being a real RPG. Long conversations. Moral ambiguity. Slow-burn character arcs. Consequences that aren’t neatly color-coded good or evil. It trusts the player to engage with the world instead of constantly jingling keys in front of them.

BG3 feels like what happens when a studio is allowed to make something ambitious without sanding off all the rough edges that make RPGs memorable in the first place. Absolute all-timer.

I should've written this a long time ago, but oh, well.

I do really think that this game deserved some of its praise back in the day (mostly 'cause of lack of competition, honestly), but finishing it left such a bittersweet taste in my mouth that i can't truly call it a „masterpiece for ages“.

I think i do understand the core vision of developers. Larian tried to ensure that this game will translate pure, chaotic DnD experience: and, I'll be frank, they somewhat did it with the outstanding turn-based combat system and all the possibilities that comes with it. Unfortunately, they failed on the other aspect that makes TTRPG have it's own renown: freedom of choice, being whoever you like to be and the consequences of it.

Storyline, and thus the choices that this game is kindly offering, have been written in such a straightforward and dichotomical way that you are either Mr. Goody-Two-Shoes or a pure offspring of Satan (wink-wink) with no real choices in between. The problem is not with the idea itself, but with it realization: whatever you choose, you'll ride on the same railroad over and over again with no differences that really matters on a global, narrative scale. Moreover, this game simply punishes you for picking granted conventionally evil choices and robs you out of possible content with nothing in return. The only consequences is, sadly, the amount of XP you'll gain and alive characters that you'll meet as the main quest goes on, i'm afraid. 

The overall quality of writing dissatisfies as well, granting a generally promising, albeit not without flaws, Act One and delving deeper into mediocrity as the story progresses further in Act Two and Three, with the second being a strange, linear filler and third an unpolished disappointment with big chunks of planned content removed in a hurry. 

And the characters? Sadly, with some exceptions they all seem more like humanized, basic fantasy archetypes/alignment charts put on screen rather than living persons with interesting, properly designed backstories and character depth/development (i'm talking about you, Wyll). And if the Act One tries to keep that a little secret, enriching the game with a bunch of popping out of nowhere party banter, interactions, random events and intrigue, well... later all of it slowly starts to disappear as you'll come closer to Baldur's Gate itself. 

But does that REALLY matter in the case of enjoying that game? No, i think not. To be honest, I've enjoyed every last bit of it, playing all day and night long in search of fun that this game perfectly delivers. What saddens me the most is the possibilities of what would've been if the game was delayed for a couple of years for extra polishing, and if the cut Early Access content/story hadn't been cut so unwisely. 

Alas, it is what it is, and despite the fact that I left a negative review, I do think that's up to you to try BG3 out and decide everything for yourself, although you should severely lower your expectations if you're looking for role-playing experience and an interesting story: you'll have nothing of that. But you'll have Minthara.

Regarding prevailing evaluations, I contend that BG3 is an exceptionally well-crafted game, yet ultimately constrained by excessive structural rigidity.

While the game offers substantial exposure to the practical mechanics of DnD, it falls short of delivering the degree of agency typically associated with the genre. Although such restriction may be justified as a compromise to accommodate novice players or to streamline development, the resulting experience is overly prescriptive and limits genuine player autonomy.

The narrative architecture is predominantly linear and unidirectional. Consequently, players are confronted with a dilemma: either compromise immersion—an essential expectation in CRPGs—by exhaustively completing side content despite the urgent narrative premise of a mind flayer parasite, or engage in repeated playthroughs with alternative characters. In the latter case, players are compelled to enact decisions that may contradict prior moral alignments or emotional investments, thereby undermining narrative coherence and experiential continuity.

The core design deficiency lies in the absence of a meaningful post-narrative state. Unlike The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, which permits continued exploration in a decompressed, post-resolution environment, or Red Dead Redemption 2, where narrative succession is achieved through a character such as John Marston, BG3 terminates the player’s progression abruptly upon completion of the main storyline. This design choice is neither sufficiently foreshadowed nor mitigated.

As a result, the relational bonds formed with companions, along with the accumulated value of equipment and progression systems, are rendered functionally obsolete. The player’s sustained investment—both affective and strategic—is effectively nullified at the moment of narrative closure. What remains is a diminished incentive structure, wherein the only recourse is to re-engage with previously unexperienced content through repetition rather than organic continuation.

This structural limitation significantly attenuates the game’s long-term experiential depth and undermines the durability of player engagement.

A superb CRPG set in the Dungeons and Dragons universe, featuring fantastic combat, locations, designs, story, and characters - highly recommended.

Create your own custom character from a variety of D&D races and classes, creating some really stunning looking characters via the creator tools, before setting out on an absolutely memorable adventure. Play as a person captured by mindflayers, implanted with mindflayer larvae aboard a flying ship called a Nautiloid, escaping with the assistance of a being trapped within an artifact known as the Astral Prism. Crash land on the outskirts of Baldur's Gate, gathering together a band of unlikely heroes - old and new - in your quest to rid yourselves of the mindflayer tadpoles wriggling in your brain. 

Baldur's Gate 3 does a fantastic job translating the Dungeon and Dragons 5e ruleset into an easy to use, easy to read, toolset as a foundation for your gameplay experience. As you and your party work their way through your adventure, you will continually be making dice rolls in order to pass a wide variety of different skill checks both in and out of combat. Walking around can trigger checks for insight, history, religion, and traps as your characters take in the situation and environment around them, lending additional information or choices for dialogue. Many people can be persuaded, intimidated, or deceived in conversations, granting you access to restricted areas, avoiding combat, gaining allies, or influencing the decisions of others in a critical moment. Depending on how you handle encounters, you might end up leaving a trail of bodies in your wake, leaving behind future allies and ending quest chains early. Locks can be picked, traps can be detected and disabled, pockets can be picked, and even hidden objects, compartments, and switches can be found. The world can be manipulated in a few different ways to get a quest completed, as combat isn't always the only option left to you; sometimes you can get by using spells, potions, conversation or manipulating the environment. Inventory is easily managed, as things can be sent back to your camp at any time, making weight management a breeze when looting bodies, carrying gold (which has weight), and collecting rare / legendary items. 

Companions are a big improvement over the ones in Divinity: Original Sin II; although my only point of contention is how badly, and immediately, every single one of them, regardless of gender or connection, wants the main character's ♥♥♥♥. From the way people react to the player character it is like he has the bestest, most magical ♥♥♥♥ in all the land, and everybody wants a turn. 

Outside of that one little tidbit, characters are well written, each with their own personality, problems, and wants that can be fulfilled during the course of your adventure. Companions can be killed, part ways with the main character, or simply never found at all, which was the case with Gale during my playthrough - somehow I completely missed interacting with him. 

There are six companions that count as origin companions, and can be selected as a playable character if you don't want to make your own:

[list]
[*] Astarion - a high elf rogue who is also a vampire spawn, seeking revenge against the vampire who sired him
[*] Gale - a human wizard, someone I completely missed in my playthrough and can't comment on
[*] Karlach - a tiefling barbarian, the one I romanced, best girl with the heart of a demonic engine
[*] Lae'zel - a githyanki fighter, seeking to free the true prince of her people and overthrow the lich queen leading her race
[*] Shadowheart - High half-elf Cleric of Shar - seeking to appease her God
[*] Wyll - a human Warlock who has made a contract with a demon, seeking to be released from it
[/list]

There are four more companions that you can encounter in your travels, two being new and two being from previous Baldur's Gate titles:

[list]
[*] Halsin - a Wood Elf Druid seeking to remove a deadly shadow fog from an area of land
[*] Jaheira - a high half-elf Druid working to fight against the Absolute, also a returning character from a previous Baldur's Gate title
[*] Minsc (and Boo!) - a human Ranger working alongside Jaheira, being a fan favourite returning from Baldur's Gate II
[*] Minithara - a Lolth-Sworn paladin drow that I ended up killing and can't comment on
[/list]

Each one has their own character side quest that you can complete, having repercussions on the story, events, and characters going forward through the three acts of the game. 

Combat is based on initiative to dictate who ends up going in what order. Characters each have their own amount of distance they can cover each turn, being able to jump and dash as an action to cover more distance or reach different levels on terrain. Melee and ranged attacks have a certain percentage to hit, that percentage being increased by certain skills and conditions placed upon both you and the enemy. Spells also fall under the percentage to hit, having a certain amount of chance to be cast successfully depending on an opponents resistances. Certain spells require concentration in order to be maintained and can be interrupted by an attack if you fail a saving throw. Certain classes like fighters can absolutely overpower and slaughter a room full of enemies quite easily, or bring down a single challenging foe with multiple heavy damage attacks. Spells - outside of scrolls - require a prepared spell slot of its spell level, or higher, in order to be cast; spells also need to be memorized before they can be used, with only so many slots available for memorization. 

Story-wise the game is quite well written, keeping me engaged the whole way through, and genuinely invested in some of my companions (especially my big red smashy tiefling GF), where I would have been legitimately upset if something happened to one of them. Each act is quite good at having it's own contained section of events, while adding to the escalating threat as a whole that needs to be addressed by the party. 

Visually, Baldur's Gate 3 is an absolute feast for the eyes; locations, environments, characters, armour sets, spells, and more are all absolutely gorgeous. People you encounter have a wide variety of looks, colourings, and simple little details that set them out and apart from anyone else you might encounter. I deeply wish I could play as a Kobold, as they remind me so hard of the gremlins from the film Gremlins, and I love everything about that.

The soundtrack is another area of quality, having numerous instrumental and vocal tracks that absolutely slap. I would go so far as to say this is one I wouldn't mind owning on vinyl even. Composers really went above and beyond when it came to putting together the pieces for specific points in the story to lift things up and elevate the whole experience. 

This is easily one of the best games I have played in the past year, one I would recommend to anyone regardless of your interest in specific genres of gaming. Baldur's Gate 3 might be one of the few games that I have seen draw in all sorts of players from across the hobby of gaming, regardless of personal likes, and still deliver a fantastic experience to them all.

Clearly a lot of people really like this game and that is great, however for me personally, despite having put over 100 hours in; trying different combinations of class and race hoping that something would click and also watching a number of guides and trying things out, it just hasn't caught my imagination.  The main things that have turned me away are:

1. Turn based combat.  I'm not against turn based gameplay in things like strategy games where you controlling things at a higher or perhaps broader level, but for this type of game, it makes combat feel slow and clunky.  That may just be because I associate this style of game with an action RPG and so my expectation is for real-time combat.

2.  Dice roll RNG.  I think for table top D&D using dice does makes sense.  However, whilst there are rules in place, table top involves real people and the DM and players can use their imagination to work around the results of dice throws in order to keep the story moving.  In game, there are a finite number of outcomes that can be programmed and all that ends up happening is either the outcome ends up being the same regardless of the route you take to get there, or you permanently lose out on something or you end up resorting to saving and reloading until you get the result you want.

3. Having to control all party members. At the start of the game you get to create a single character. This can take some time, the result of which means you feel a connection and investment in that character.  However, once the game gets going you begin to pick up new party members.  Those are pre-made characters who you don't really have an investment in but are expected to level and control all the same.  I would have preferred if either you could create all the characters yourself (which wouldn't work as the story revolves around the game knowing their backstories and they are obviously in the cut scenes), or there was an option for the computer to control those characters leaving you to focus on your own character.

4. Due to the nature of this being an implementation of table top D&D, movement is restricted.  This applies both inside and outside of combat. However, outside of combat those restrictions feel, well, restrictive. Characters move at what feels like snail pace. Moving through water slows a character down even further, which seems a bit pointless when outside of combat.  Even when terrain clearly looks like it could easily be traversed, you may not be able move in that direction (including jumping) because it is outside of the allowed path.  For me, this breaks the immersion.

5. Characters in your party can be left behind.  Occasionally, a party member will get stuck or just not have the available movement to stay with the party.  If that happens it is up to you to notice and go back for them or swap to that character to bring them forwards.  If the party members are selected to be grouped then I expect them to either keep together or for some notification to be given to let you know if one is left behind.  It's a small gripe, but irritating none the less.

6. Genitalia. I realise D&D is meant to be a game of imagination but the inclusion of genitalia in an RPG computer game, rather than seeming clever, funny or innovative, just feels a little 'oh dear, how sad'.  There is an option to turn it off at least.

I have given this game so, so many chances. I even convinced myself that I liked it for a time but there are just too many little issues that make this game frustratingly unplayable for me. Controller support is not very good and what's crazy is that it's *really* good in Divinity Original Sin II, so I know Larian can do it. But comparing the controller interface to the keyboard/mouse in this game is just infuriating. When using a keyboard everything is very organized and it's easy to separate different types of spells/powers which can help when deciding what to do on your turn, but on controller you only have a row of radials with no clear organization and minimal indicators as to the cost of using these powers. I would have to spend a lot of time manually organizing my radials into something usable whereas in Divinity, spells are placed on a hotbar where it's easy to arrange them and see exactly what they do. It's possible some of this comes from the unholy matrimony of D&D 5e mechanics and video game design limitations but it's so frustrating that I just play keyboard/mouse. I guess that's fine, but, like, this game is available (and more expensive) on consoles where controller is the only option. Now something that I know is 5e's fault, is that combat is not very fun. It's okay, but Divinity combat is INCREDIBLE to the extend in which I look forward to encounters. In BG3 I dread them, not because they're especially hard (Divinity is MUCH harder) but because they're just boring. On top of that there's very little reason to be careful with resources or spell slots because you can long rest pretty much whenever you want with no consequences. Now, of course, there are little quality of life changes that make BG3 a step above DOSII in some ways, and I'm not going to pretend like the cutscene animations aren't super cool, because they are. This game is beautiful, no doubt about that. But my biggest issue, which makes all the little improvements worthless, is that I just can't play the game. I have spent hours, literally HOURS  just trying to join multiplayer sessions. And even when I can finally get in, the game crashes so often that it feels like there's always an expiration date on any fun I'm having. Not to mention the MASSIVE file size which just feels so ridiculously bloated and makes file verification (which I'm constantly having to run) take forever. What's crazy is that the game was working a few months ago, consistently for the first time since I started playing, and then they released a patch which broke everything all over again???? Why, WHY is this game *almost* incredible but just incapable of fumbling at the last second!? I will probably continue to give this game more chances, because it just occupies that much of my soul, but I do not recommend this game to new players. It's too much of a headache. So I finally dived into Baldurs Gate 3 and holy crap my life is basically over. I havent slept properly in days and my brain is completely rotted by dice rolls. If you havent played this yet what are you even doing with your life??

The absolute best part about this game is the mindblowing amount of freedom. The devs at Larian are actual geniuses or maybe just insane because they literally thought of EVERYTHING. You can try the most unhinged, stupid, or downright evil stuff and the game just looks at you and says "yup, lets see how that plays out." There is no invisible walls telling you how to play. Good choice? Works. Horrible, chaotic, smoothbrain choice? Also somehow works and leads to unique stuff.

Like, I tried doing a classic machine gun spell caster setup on one run, but then on another I just started messing around. At one point, I accidentally dropped a literal entire monastery structure on a certain pale, sassy friend of mine... and instead of a game over screen or a glitch, he just gave me the most hilarious, unhinged verbal beatdown about the concentrated power of the sun once I brought him back. It was golden.

Another time, I was getting absolutely wrecked in a fight, so I just started chucking bottles of grease everywhere. Watching these incredibly imposing, terrifying bosses just straight up slip on a puddle of grease and immediately end their turn completely helpless is the funniest ♥♥♥♥ ever. Oh, and if you ever find an old man standing by a dirt road who looks suspisiously like he belongs in a wizard retirement home, just tell him to keep moving. The game handles it perfectly. Or when the narrator sounds like a tired dungeon master who is completely sick of your crap because you decided to backtalk a magical mirror.

The reactivity is just unmatched. Every time I think "surely the devs didnt code a reaction for this specific flavor of chaos," they prove me wrong. It rewards you for being clever, but it rewards you even more for being a absolute menace.

Honestly it's easily an 11/10. Some minor bugs here and there but nothing that ruins the experience. If you like rpgs or just want to see how far you can push a game before it breaks, buy it now. Just prepare to say goodbye to your social life.

I am a big fan of RPGs; basically every single one of my favorite games is an RPG. So when I heard about a new critically acclaimed RPG that was released, I immediately bought it. In retrospect, that was obviously a bad decision. I am someone who cares first and foremost about gameplay and consistently doesn’t like games whose main selling point is their story. I don’t like the D&D system; I love roleplaying, but the mechanics D&D uses to simulate roleplay and combat make it actively less fun than just roleplaying with no rules at all. If I thought about it for even a moment, I would have realized this wasn’t going to be a game for me. But I didn’t. I had two playthroughs, the first I quit after completing Act 1, and the second I managed to finish the game  On the surface this game has all the things you’d want from an RPG, exploring areas, filling out your map, beating enemies, collecting items, completing quests; lots of little hits of dopamine that make it easy to keep going. But when I really think of the quality of each of these aspects, they aren’t very good. First, and the only one I don’t mind, exploring the world is enjoyable. There are lots of hidden items to find and areas to explore. My only complaint would be that it got a bit overwhelming at times with how much exploring and options I was given. Next, beating enemies, my second least favorite part of the game. As stated, I don’t like the D&D’s combat system. I feel it does a bad job of simulating real time combat and the combat isn’t very fun. BG3 is a video game though, so turn-based combat is normal. However, I personally don’t like the initiative order system; initiative is easily the biggest determiner of how well you’ll do in a fight, so it’s annoying that something that important is random. There’s a reason why most RPGs either have you and the enemy alternating attacks, or have everyone’s attacks refresh on timers, it makes the combat much more strategy based, which is what you want for turn based combat. In general though, BG3’s combat is way too random, with how likely you are to hit and how much damage you do. You could replay the same fight with the same strategy over and over again and get vastly different results. Yes, you do want some randomness in a combat system so that it isn’t a solved game, but BG3 has just way too much randomness for my liking. In general, enemies don’t really have weaknesses or special attacks; most combats feel very similar to each other, boiling every fight down to just draining the collective HP pool, and once you figure out the best ways to do that, you’ve basically trivialized the whole combat system. I have more gripes with the combat system, but I don’t want this review to run too long, just know it is easily the worst RPG combat system I’ve experienced and is not fun. As for my least favorite part about the game, it’s collecting items, which might just be a thing only I care about. Typically, RPGs do one of two things. Either they have a bunch of basic loot scattered about, or have lots of unique loot across the map with in-game ways of helping you find it, both are completely valid ways of doing loot. BG3 on the other hand had a crap ton of unique loot all over the place with no built-in way of helping you find it. I am a loot goblin, and I enjoy picking up everything, but there is no good way of tracking loot you’ve gotten and finding loot that you’ve missed. You either have to heavily explore every area when you enter it or use a guide, otherwise you will miss a lot of stuff and have no way of knowing what you missed. For example, I was doing a thrower build for Karlach, and there was a weapon that I wanted to get. I ended up having to reload a save because the guy who sells that weapon leaves if Shadowheart is your party, which she was. Like, I didn’t even know that guy was a vendor. It’s way too easy to miss loot in this game. Also, I hate how so much of the best loot are from shopkeepers; I want to find the really cool loot, I don’t want to just buy it off some guy. BG3 is clearly made for people to only find some of the loot, which sucks for people who enjoy collecting loot like me. I mean, so many games feature collectathons for a reason. Anywho, BG3’s lack of care for loot goblins like me made exploring feel like a real chore. And finally there are the quests, which I personally wasn’t a big fan of, but I can see why people are. I was never able to get invested in the world, and while I enjoyed the characters well enough, the slight joy I got from these characters was vastly offset by how little I enjoyed the gameplay. Whenever I dislike the gameplay in a game, it makes it hard for me to care about the game’s other aspects, and BG3 is no exception. Although, I do have a couple of actual complaints about the quests. First is that in Act 1 nothing you did really progressed the story at all, heck you can just walk up to the mountains and pretty much skip the whole thing, it made the first few dozens hours of the game feel like it had little momentum. Second is that Act 3 has way too many quests, like I only got through half of Baldur’s Gate and I already have like 20 side quests, some of which would require me to go into the second half of the city and pick up even more side quests, I just got way too overwhelmed. I feel like they could’ve paced the quests better so that you’re finishing some as you get new ones. Overall, I don’t have much to say about the quests, I’ve experienced far better and far worse. And finally, in terms of the story, which everyone seems to adore, I don’t really see what’s so great about it. It’s overall a pretty simple story, with you just travelling from place to place, helping random people, killing bad guys, until you eventually get to the ending. It was a pretty standard RPG story. And in terms of choices you can make, there almost always two options, one good one and one evil one. Sometimes the choices you are given are more morally ambiguous, but for the most part if you are doing a good or evil playthrough, you only really have one choice. And of course, the majority of the game is exploring, fighting, side quests, etc. So even if you did a second playthrough of the game, the vast majority of the game would be identical, with only minor things changing. Of course, this isn’t a problem, most RPGs don’t have branching stories, but with how much emphasis this game puts on roleplaying, I expected a bit more options to make the character feel like my own. So overall, the exploration was enjoyable, but collecting loot wasn’t fun, the combat is boring and has way too much randomness, the quests and characters are alright but nothing to right home about, and the story is pretty standard. As always with games critically acclaimed for their story, I fail to see the hype. 6.5/10

I'd heard so much praise about this game, I finally decided to give it a try. I've been playing a lot of immersive, story-rich RPGs: Kingdom Come 2, a replay of The Witcher 3, etc. Everyone kept telling me that I had to play BG3. I'd been hoping it would go on sale but finally gave in to the hype and bought it at full price.

And I kind of hate it? 

I kept hearing everyone say how immersive it is, but I find it to be the opposite of immersion. That's due in large part to the classic RPG style, and how I'm constantly having to interact with very specific menus and systems and inventories in a way that almost becomes invisible in other games. That's not to my taste, but I can't fault the game for being what it is.

The other reason I have a hard time with immersion is that your character doesn't speak during dialogue. This makes every conversation feel awkward, and I never get a feel for my character actually existing. They're just an avatar. Which, yes, I know all video game characters are in a literal sense. But most games allow me to feel that the player character has a personality and wants and hopes, largely from the performance of the voice actor, and that informs the decisions I make while playing that character. Without their dialogue, it doesn't ever feel like they actually exist. Which again breaks immersion for me. And also makes me wonder why we even had the option of choosing a voice for them in the first place.

The enemy AI is very, very stupid. Maybe this is because I just played Kingdom Come 2, where NPCs will notice a door in their house open at night and so look around to see if anything is missing, then remember you were snooping around and come look for you. But I've had several encounters in BG3 where during the fight I just close a door on half the enemies and, instead of opening it, they just shoot arrows at the closed doors while I kill their friends.

I just finished Act One, so maybe this gets better, but I also feel like the choices made and the game's overall reactivity aren't very good. I'd heard your choices matter so much in this game, but NPCs will tell me things I never did, make assumptions over big choices where I chose differently, and even tell me we'd made plans together earlier when this is the first time I'm meeting them.

The voice acting is pretty stellar for the NPCs, but the writing is lackluster and juvenile. I can get past that to a certain extent (I love the original VtM Bloodlines, for instance, so some cheesy writing and jank can be fun) but it just runs counter to my expectations for the game due to all the praise it received. I find the characters to be pretty two dimensional. And for all the different races and classes in the game, there's no sense of "culture" among the different groups. The Tieflings live and speak and act exactly like the humans and the halflings and so on. Only the Goblins (enemy NPCs) seem distinct in any way.

It's also very combat heavy. I try to find a way around combat as much as I can, but most encounters force you into combat, even though my stealth and social stats are very high. I'd hoped for more choice and variation.

I'm hoping to find a way to appreciate the game more, but I am pretty baffled at all the praise and awards it's received. It's not an awful game by any means, but it also comes nowhere near the praise it's received.

tl;dr - Make sure you know what kind of game to expect when playing this and that it's the type of game you're into before buying, and don't let the praise make you think you're getting something on the level of the best games you've ever played. My dislike of this game is not just due to its faults but also my expectations before playing it.

[h1]Baldur’s Gate 3 Review – The Horniest Camp in Faerûn[/h1]

Baldur’s Gate 3 is, from a technical standpoint, an achievement.
Full performance capture, cinematic dialogue, seamless co-op, and a level of polish most RPGs never reach. It feels like the new benchmark.

And the combat deserves the praise.
This is the best turn-based DnD implementation ever made. Encounters reward planning. Builds, rolls, and positioning matter. It finally feels like tabletop logic translated into a digital space without losing depth.

If this review were only about systems, it would end here on a high note.

[h2]The Story That Never Dares[/h2]

The problem is the narrative.

For a game this large and this celebrated, the story plays it remarkably safe. The structure is familiar, the twists are visible from miles away, and the moral conflicts rarely force you into uncomfortable territory. It wants to be epic, but it avoids being unsettling. It gestures toward boldness without fully committing to it.

The villains suffer most from this caution.

[spoiler]Ketheric Thorm is framed as a tragic, god-touched warlord whose presence should reshape the world around him. Instead, much of his impact is delivered through exposition and brooding speeches before culminating in a fairly conventional boss encounter. The supposed avatar of dread ends up feeling like a raid boss with a tragic backstory rather than a transformative force in the narrative.[/spoiler]

The scale is large. The risk is not.

[h2]Companions Built for Applause[/h2]

The companions are memorable, but often in a performative way. They are designed to stand out immediately. Big personalities. Strong aesthetics.

Yet over time, some arcs begin to feel predictable. Shadowheart’s internal conflict repeats familiar beats for long stretches. Astarion’s trauma-laced charm oscillates between vulnerability and theatrical sarcasm in ways that feel engineered for reaction rather than discovery. They are not shallow characters.

But they often feel curated for engagement rather than organically unfolding.

[h2]The Horniest Camp in Faerûn[/h2]

And then we arrive at camp. The emotional center of the story. The place where bonds should deepen naturally over shared struggle.

Instead, it often feels like the Forgotten Realms’ most efficient speed-dating retreat.

The world is on the brink of annihilation. You have a mind flayer tadpole in your skull. Gods are scheming. Empires are shaking. And somehow, within what feels like a long weekend, half your party is ready to discuss eternal devotion.

It stops feeling like chemistry and starts feeling like a triggered dialogue tree. Intimacy accelerates at a pace that undermines tension. Emotional payoff is replaced by availability. The result is tonal whiplash. Apocalypse outside the tent. Romance queue inside it.

[h2]An Ending That Should Have Roared[/h2]

After dozens of hours, the finale arrives with competence but not with weight. It resolves threads, it ties off arcs, but it rarely challenges the player in a way that feels transformative. For a narrative centered around identity, manipulation, and cosmic stakes, the conclusion feels restrained.

[h2]Buyer’s Regret Verdict[/h2]

Baldur’s Gate 3 is mechanically outstanding and technically industry-leading. As a systems-driven RPG, it deserves recognition. As a DnD combat experience, it sets a standard.

But story and companion writing undermine the atmosphere it tries to build. The ambition in presentation is not matched by ambition in narrative risk.

Wow...where do I even begin?

I want to start by saying that I have nothing but love and respect for Larian.  Divinity: Original Sin 2 is one of my favorite video games of all time, easily top 10 and maybe even top 5, and every time traces of that game shine through in BG3, a genuine smile appears on my face.  Then a moment later I get reminded that this is a D&D game, based on D&D rules, and the smile vanishes, because I realize I could be playing DOSE2 for the 30th time instead and having much, much more fun.

Baldur's Gate 3 sucks, but not because BG3 itself sucks.  Rather, it sucks because only getting to cast 5 fireballs per long rest sucks.  It sucks because having 28 STR and still failing a STR check in act 1 on normal difficulty because the dice decided to f**k you sucks.  It sucks because utility spells like teleports still consume limited per-rest slots even when you cast them outside combat, which limits exploration hard.  BG3 sucks because it's a D&D game with D&D rules, and D&D rules absolutely, completely, and totally suck.  They suck all the fun out of what could have been, and should have been, the greatest game ever made.

And I know this because DOSE2 shows what happens when Larian doesn't have to stick to a D&D rulebook.  DOSE2 is an unequivocally better video game.  In DOSE2, cooldowns are turn-based, which translates to 1 second per turn outside combat.  Thus, when you want to teleport outside combat, then do it again, you just have to wait 8 seconds.  This is long enough to get caught by patrolling enemies, if you plan poorly or just get unlucky, but you can still do it.  Character stats are also made in a way that actually makes sense - if your character has 28 STR and the check only requires 20, you pass the check, period, full stop.  You only have a dice roll when you don't surpass the threshold - so if the check requires 30 STR, THEN you have a chance of failure, but EVEN THEN that chance is based on the difference between your stat and the check.  So in this example, your 28 STR would still give you a 93% chance of success.  In BG3, your odds would either be completely random or a 100% chance of failure, but in DOSE2, you can spend stat points such that even if you can't guarantee success, you can directly dictate what your odds are.

I know a lot of people have said "trust the dice."  Well, I don't.  I tried to.  I've completed Act 1 of this game 3 times now, including every single side quest.  And no less than seven times, my character with 30 in every core stat and advantage in several areas still somehow managed to fail a dice roll.  I'm sorry, but I cheated myself a god character and the game STILL found a way to f**k me over.  Any ruleset that allows a character with maximum stats to fail ANYTHING is an inherently flawed ruleset, whether I trust it or not.

So I'm done with this thing.  I don't regret buying it and won't ask for a refund, but only because I love Larian and I am confident that the next Divinity game will be absolutely, positively amazing.  But I will never play this again.  Never.  Why would I, when I could just play DOSE2 again and have a better experience all around?

This can be noticed as early as chapter one, but it is painfully obvious by the time you reach Baldur's Gate, some characters pretty much have their arc mostly complete and you have to wade through a couple more encounters to actually finish them.
