I love BG3 overall, and I still think Astarion’s romance with Tav/Dark Urge is beautifully written, especially with Dark Urge. That route feels polished, emotionally coherent, and deeply connected to the story.

But Origin Karlach/Astarion has serious continuity problems that broke the romance for me.

Karlach/Astarion is a very strong concept in theory. Karlach cannot be touched, while Astarion’s Act 1 romance usually relies on seduction, physical intimacy, and using desire as a survival strategy. This should make their romance unique, because his usual tools should not work on her the same way. Instead, it often feels like the regular Astarion romance with Karlach-specific patches that do not fully fit.

A few examples:

1. In Act 1, Astarion tries to bite Karlach. That part is easier to understand because he is starving and desperate. But later at the tiefling party, he still suggests “a night of passion” as if Karlach were a regular Tav, even though he already knows she cannot be touched. This could have worked if the scene clearly framed it as his usual seduction script failing because of her engine, but as written, it just feels like the game forgets Karlach’s condition.

2. Instead of sleeping together in Act 1, they only talk. But the next morning she wakes up naked, as if the standard romance scene still happened. This contradicts the entire point of the scene.

3. After Karlach’s engine is upgraded and she can finally touch people (Was Act 2 for me), Astarion gives a generic line about shaking her hand because she might snap him in two, instead of a real romantic payoff. This should be one of the most important emotional moments for this pairing.

4. Astarion’s confession still says his plan was to seduce her, sleep with her, and manipulate her feelings. That works for Tav/Dark Urge, but it does not work for Karlach, because sleeping with her was impossible in Act 1.

5. The romance keeps wobbling between “they can’t touch” and “they can touch now,” depending on the scene. This makes the relationship feel inconsistent rather than intentionally restrained.

There are simple ways this could be fixed. Karlach could wake up clothed after the Act 1 talk scene. Astarion’s party dialogue and confession could be adjusted for Karlach, focusing on failed seduction/emotional manipulation instead of sex being a realistic option. The Act 2 engine upgrade could trigger a proper romantic reaction, even a reused kiss animation would be better than the generic handshake line. Or the major touch payoff could be delayed until Act 3 and tied into Astarion’s graveyard scene, which would actually fit Karlach beautifully.

The execution feels incomplete. I reached Act 2 and lost interest in continuing this playthrough because the spell broke. I hope this route gets polished, because Karlach/Astarion could be one of the most interesting romances in the game.

Upvote or Downvote can mean either loving or hating a game. Few see anything inbetween.

This game is inbetween for me, but leans negatively.

The positives are the incredible level of visual polish. It's a very polished game. All the technical elements are well done. I'll say that.

The negatives, though, are quite numerous, but they aren't all equally negative. Let's start with the obvious. This game is oozing woke ideology. Even if it won't say it out right, it's there, for all to see. It starts when you create a character, and the gender is separated from the sex. Want to be a woman with a penis? Go right ahead. Nevermind that it makes no sense in the setting. Never mind that it's an example of going out of one's way to cater to a very vocal and insane minority of people at the expense of reason and sanity. 

The woke doesn't end there though. Every scene feels like a Disney movie poster. They have the perfect balance of "races". Black dwarves, black elves, black this black that. Does it matter that dwarves evolved to live underground where melanin is closer to a mineral than a pigment catalyst? Not to Larian or WotC. They care more about virtue signaling than they do creating cohesive and meaningful cultures. All they see is skin color. They don't see subtle cultural differences, the tendency of certain races to naturally share traits which make sense to be inherited by their environment and nature. They throw all of that away to make sure that every gender and racial make up of humans is represented in every "race" or species in the game. It's stupid, childish, and down right disturbing. 

Because their idea of "diversity" is to throw a paint bucket on one of every character type in the game, it is to be expected that the actual meaningful types of diversity, such as thought, personality, interests, passions etc were ignored. Instead, it's only surface deep. Vapid, vain , and superficial differences are all the wokesters care about because they are what they claim to hate. This leads to very mundane, stale, and underdeveloped characters.

It's so hard to take the setting seriously because of the ridiculous colorswap skin color focused , gender bending characters. They look, feel, and act more like caricatures of real people than real people. Feeling any connection for them is out the window, with the exception of maybe two in the whole game. 

Further still, every character is bi, and every character wants to have sex with you after even a single nice word is thrown their way. It's jarring to be talking to a clearly straight character, only to have the narrator suggest we start having sex with eachother in only two dialogue exchanges. This might not seem like a big deal, but it will totally ruin characters for you when they are presented one way, then instantaneously given an abrupt 180 personality shift. Many such instances of this happening soured my opinion of the character to the point I just don't like talking to them. Add in the ridiculous skin color swapping and gender bending, you end up with a cast of characters better suited for the looney troons than a semi-serious RPG.

Moving on from the blatant political bent, the rest of the game suffers from a similar lack of meaningful nuance. Abilities all feel very similarly. Spells more or less offer different colors of the same few effects. Spamming the same few spells over and over, because they're clearly the most effective, gets old pretty fast. Combat in general begins to feel the same after a while. Fights move along methodically and predictably. Occasionally someone will crit, but the fights feel stale and lifeless. Turn based combat is rigid, inflexible, and creates odd situations.

Effects lack conviction. Most everything is just a couple turns in length. The odds of spells being resisted is high. There's not much satisfaction to the spell system at all really. 

Overall, the game lacks a feeling of urgency and lethality that would make the moment to moment combat more exhilarating. Instead, Fights move along in predictable fashion, with predictable outcomes, and predictable rewards. 

Having to rest every other fight wouldn't be so bad if the player wasn't forced to return to camp, requiring a level load out of their area, where they must then get past a few animations before they can rest. The process to rest adds tedium which quickly gets old, but always forces you to to do it. How great it would be to click a button and instantly just be rested up, with no loss to the challenge or value of the experience. The old BG games worked that way. It was a much better and more streamlined system.

Unlike other great Crpgs, the handholding removes much of the mystery from the game. Virtually every trap is automatically discovered. Their effects are typically minor, and the ability to disarm them is almost guaranteed with a default party. There's hardly anything left to the player's imagination, nor their senses. Hidden switches are easily seen, chests easily opened, most fights easily won. There are few interesting puzzles, though they do exist. The original Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 had far more detailed hidden item searching, where player agency mattered as much as the character. Baldur's Gate 3 does not think highly enough of the player to expect them to overcome adversity, so they give very little of it. 

The camera sucks. Controlling the Camera is tedious. Being 3D, it requires constant re-orientation and positioning. Oftentimes it gets stuck on walls, ramps, doorways or any other background asset.  I can't remember the last time I played a CRPG where the Camera fought me as much as the enemies did. 

Most CRPGs allow for seamless and fast switching of characters. Due to the turn based nature, each character must be resolved in order. While splitting party members up is possible, it's problematic. Characters can't be group selected, so each character must be controlled individually when group  mode is deactivated. Furthermore, every character has their own inventory, which is completely disorganized. It's just one giant x by y grid of item slots. Trying to find a specific item, on a specific character is downright obnoxious. The low contrast, dark color of the UI does not help with this. I've gone hours without even wanting to go  looking for items. It's easier to simply not care.

Finally, my least favorite mechanic by far is the die rolling system. Ultimately, this is what stalled my playthrough more than anything else. The ridiculousness of forcing me to click on a 20 sided die to resolve virtually every in game challenge is unfathomable. The game will have you rolling a die every minute, on average. Some rooms are so full of traps and treasure, characters will be rolling dice for minutes. First, a screen pops up, interrupting your flow. You then have to determine which modifiers you want applied to the roll. Then you click the die to roll it. Now you wait for the die to finish its flashy roll animation. Once that ends, it starts another animation adding your mondifiers together one by one ( could be 5 or more often). After this ends, it gives the result in a final flashy animation and tells you either you succeeded or failed.... this happens every..single..time... you want to open a locked chest, disarm a trap, convince an npc, pull a stuck lever... etc etc. You'll watch this same animation 1000 times over dozens of hours. This should have, and could have been done behind the scenes without the player even knowing.

BG3,despite all of its polish, has only superficial depth in both the setting and gameplay. They cleaned and polished every speck of character out of whatever this game claims itself to be. Whether its the repetitive combat, or the vain, skin deep woke pandering, BG3 just feels bland. While I don't love it, I also don't feel enough about it to hate it.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is one of the best RPGs I have ever played, and after nearly 300 hours, I can confidently say it deserves the praise it gets. It combines strong storytelling, tactical turn-based combat, meaningful exploration, and incredible artistic design into one massive experience. While it has a few flaws, they are nowhere near enough to take away from what makes the game special.

The story and roleplaying are easily some of the game’s greatest strengths. The choices you make feel meaningful, whether they affect your companions, quests, or the larger world around you. The characters are well-written, memorable, and full of personality, making it easy to become invested in their stories. Even smaller side quests often feel important because of the writing and the way the game reacts to your decisions.

The turn-based combat is another major highlight. It rewards strategy, creativity, and experimentation rather than just rushing into every fight. Positioning, spell choices, environmental effects, and party builds all matter, which makes battles feel satisfying and unique. The combat can be challenging, especially for players unfamiliar with Dungeons & Dragons mechanics, but learning the system is part of what makes the game so rewarding.

Exploration, world-building, and presentation are also outstanding. Every area feels carefully designed, filled with secrets, hidden paths, interesting characters, and lore that makes the world feel alive. The art direction, environments, music, voice acting, and character animations all add to the immersion. The game does have some technical issues, especially in later parts like Act 3, and it can occasionally feel overwhelming because of its size and complexity, but these problems are small compared to everything the game does right.

Overall, Baldur’s Gate 3 is a massive, detailed, and unforgettable RPG that sets a very high standard for storytelling and player freedom. Its few negatives, such as bugs, performance dips, or a steep learning curve, are not enough to stop me from recommending it. If you enjoy deep stories, tactical combat, meaningful choices, and a world that rewards curiosity, Baldur’s Gate 3 is absolutely worth playing.

This abomination has almost nothing in common with the original Baldur’s Gate titles and should never have been seriously considered for Game of the Year.

Black Isle Studios was an American company that understood what made Baldur’s Gate special. This modern entry comes out of Belgium, and it shows. It feels completely disconnected from the traditional spirit and tone of the series.

The deliberately debilitating camera limitations are a perfect example. You can’t even properly look up. In a modern RPG? Seriously? It feels less like a design decision and more like an artificial restriction that constantly reminds you that you’re fighting the interface instead of exploring the world.

Item and spell descriptions are vague and poorly explained, forcing players into endless trial-and-error loops. Instead of the satisfaction of figuring something out, you’re left repeating the same failures simply because the game couldn’t be bothered to communicate clearly.

And then there’s the lore. Goblins speaking perfect English? Really? Do the developers even know what a goblin is supposed to be in the Baldur’s Gate universe? The world feels like it was stitched together by people who skimmed a wiki instead of actually understanding the setting.

Where are the Gibberlings? Where’s the mad necromancer and his deranged halfling thief? Xzar and Montaron were iconic companions that gave the original games their strange charm. Instead we get characters that are forgettable at best and bizarre at worst.

And what exactly is a Githyanki doing here? It all feels less like faithful Forgotten Realms world-building and more like creative licensing run amok.

This feels less like Baldur’s Gate and more like some unrelated RPG wearing its name like a costume. It’s the equivalent of releasing a Gothic remake with no Shadowbeasts—technically you can do it, but you’ve completely missed the point.

What a waste of time and money.

Game of the Year?

The game literally rolls dice to decide whether you’re allowed to continue without reloading... that’s not depth, that’s bad design dressed up as innovation.

A huge portion of the so-called “choices” are fake. Pick the wrong dialogue, fail one arbitrary roll, and suddenly you’re trapped in an unwinnable encounter or punished with a game over. That’s not player freedom... that’s trial-and-error with extra steps.

They sold this game as some gigantic RPG with unmatched scope, but that claim falls apart the moment you actually play it. Most quests are effectively mandatory, either because the game artificially locks progression or because stepping outside the intended route gets you instantly destroyed by enemies far above your level. The result is constant paranoia: spam quicksave every few minutes because the game loves punishing exploration with cheap deaths.

And if you want proof of what this game’s audience actually values, just look at Nexus Mods. The most downloaded mods tell the whole story: most are adult mods expanding romance and sex options, and another big chunk are cheats.

A huge part of the praise comes from people who don’t care much about CRPG systems at all, they just wanted a polished fantasy dating simulator with cinematic dialogue and party members to sleep with.

Again, I was going to give it a "meh", but after struggling with its problems for hours, I'm going to outright downgrade it.  It's not a good game.  And it absolutely IS NOT one of the greatest games ever made.  Probably isn't even in the top 10 of "D&D" games ever made.

Problems include:

*RNG Bullshi...  At a certain point it no longer becomes fun to watch your characters fail to roll above a 4.  As someone who has done alpha and beta testing on games before, I can tell you that there is something wrong with their dice rolling system.

*Camera Controls.  The way you can move and control the camera is janky as hell, and absolutely frustrating.

*Interface. It's just poorly designed.  If I'm using an item from someone's inventory, if I don't have the right character selected, it uses that item for a different character.  Absolutely asinine.

*D&D Rules.  Nevermind how it's not working how it's supposed to...  It's not working how it says it's supposed to.  For example, I've watched Karlach drop out of a rage and lose it MULTIPLE TIMES despite being attacked.

*Pathfinding.  I've never seen such poor pathfinding on a modern game.  Couple this with poor camera controls, and I've often sent people way off path because I clicked on invisible terrain that the camera couldn't see.  Which leads me to the next problem...

*Lack of a pause button.  Some of these problems could be tolerable if there was a pause button.  If I was able to stop a character running off into misfortune because of the bad interface and camera, it wouldn't be as infuriating.  


I'm off to investigate if there are any mods that fix the broken RNG of this game.  If there are, I'll try again.  But I'd rather catch a testicle in a zipper than watch the game pathologically keep my rolls under 5.

The game has a lot to offer, but in it's current state, 2 years after release, if you want to roleplay as anything but what the intended path is: don't bother.

For multiple hours I've been trying to tolerate many sequence breaks, buggy triggers and wonky fights, but the breaking point is how the game punished me for having the one race that doesn't let me gain an inspiration event... let me explain:

Spoilers for Act 1:
[spoiler]So I'm Dark Urge as a Female Drow, I'm trying to roleplay as an evil character. I'm on the "goblin temple" where Gut is. So I go to the torture chamber to get a Dark Urge inspiration. The goblin tortures see me and I say to step aside and let me handle it. They obey and decide to leave the place... but I have no option to torture the prisoner. I can talk to the prisoner and get information about Halsin and the Nightsong, I can pick up the torture weapons, but I can't attack the prisoner or have a dialogue option that lets me torture him. No option as a drow allows me to torture the prisoner. So the work-around is to use Disguise Self, turn to another race and THEN the option will appear for me to torture... why? Why is this even a thing, considering Drows are basically the more intended-to-be evil aligned races in the entire game and THEY are the ones that miss out on one of the most evil actions on act 1? It's stupid on several ways, and this is a drow-exclusive interaction Larian Studios knowingly programmed without the option to torture.

And if we must point out other issues I have had so far with my playthroughs of this game: NPCs don't react to the bodies of their own kin on ground.... so basically I wanted to slaughter all the druids in the emerald grove, so I, one-by-one, sometimes two at a time, used Performance and Minor Illusion to guide them to some outside area, and repeatedly killed them outside of sight of other druids. And that way I was able to kill all druids with none of them suspecting a thing or reacting to the dead druid bodies.

I accepted to be on a romance with Lae'zel, but with no sex scene yet, it was just the flag to trigger the initial romance. When I went outside of camp, Shadowheart and Laezel were talking about how good we were on bed, even though we never did anything.

Another major issue: at night, Astarion confided to me about his vampiric nature, and I asked about Cazador and his backstory, so on... then, on the same night, the cutscene where Astarion tries to bite me plays out, and my character (and the game) act like this was a huge revelation and they did not know about it. The next morning, the same dialogue options about Cazador and his backstory were there as if I had not triggered them already, so the game got confused with flags.

It also happened that goblins have shot through walls with their arrows to hit my characters in some combat during the blighted village. And it wasn't through a window or crack, it was literal solid wood wall, a goblin was on the other side and Astarion on the other, they shot and hit me, and Astarion couldn't hit back with his bow.

I've also faced many wonky path-finding moments where my characters went through extremely long paths for something that was mere meters away from them, happened at least twice: in the goblin camp and in the dark cave below blighted village.

And there's no search option on the adventurer's chest, which can easily have over 100 items in just a few hours of exploring (which the game heavily encourages)

The game continuously makes several time-restricting scenarios/ideas in the earlygame, which would make you think you shouldn't long rest as that could mean events will happen while you sleep, but the truth is that next to nothing happens if you long rest, in fact you HAVE to if you want to progress character stories. My issue with the long rest system is that it is inversely proportional to the story's narrative and what you would think is going to happen or should happen, and the paranoia that events MIGHT happen if you long rest is completely broken when you realize they won't, such as the hyenas being pregnant with gnolls for several days or karlach being wounded and a few meters aways from her hunters for several long rests, just standing there.[/spoiler]

While I'd love to go on about every inconvenience, some minor and some major, steam has a text limit, so I'll drop here.

So, in summary, the roleplaying game has too many events and scenarios which absolutely break the roleplaying aspect of it, for too many times has my immersion been broken, and basically I can't properly play as an evil character because the game isn't built with that in mind, it's built with you being a helpful hand. I won't recommend you play it if you're as picky as I am. But otherwise it's an okay game to turn your brain off to.

I wouldn't recommend this game simply because there seems to be a blind acceptance of its heavy satanically driven content.

It desperately encourages the character to accept, which most do, transhumanism, much like Cyberpunk 2077 and numerous other corporate void games that have little in the way of meaning or morality.

It attempts to force characters and thus the player, to accept devils and demons as everyday companions - it removes the nature of morality altogether - I found that I could hack my way through a town with little or no consequence to even my public reputation. The fundamental philosophy of the game is skewed and flawed in ways that prevent the player from even attempting a basic morality.

Next are the mechanical failures of the game, which I am surprised did not bother players more - specifically the issues with the camera, which has difficulty in various areas staying on the same elevation as the player, so you are forced into a birds eye view to correct the issue. Jumping also has problems and I really didn't understand why I couldn't use rope to cross chasms.

Then there is the abandonment of the original BG series - mechanically you are no longer afforded the pleasure of live turn based combat, which is vastly superior gameplay in contrast with strict turn based gameplay. I understand that because of online group dynamics such a feat would me more challenging if a pause feature could not be implemented for groups, which it could, but that is all to say the combat system is lazy and unimaginative. If I wanted to play Original Sin I would, and I don't. Some of the longer or repeat combat scenarios are BORING!

Then comes the frantic fleeing from the best part of the BG series, character creation and classic D&D mechanics, which if you did not play D&D 35 years ago may not seem like anything important but the differences are. I do ever so hate the even ended stats system - the fact is that there was always supposed to be a great deal of variance in player stats to make the game more realistic, without the player role (diced based stat determination) in character creation its just not as fun, more bland and sterilized like the rest of the gameplay.

The characters themselves all seem to be fatherless degenerates, likely reflecting the personalities of whoever made this game - everyone is angry and bloodthirsty - and if they are righteously minded then you can be sure they have horns or are a l3sbian or something.

I did not finish the game (I got to Act III, left it running so my hours are astronomical) but the initial storyline of the brain worms was not bad but kind of desperate in its attempts to explain every solution away whilst setting up contradicting forces on each side of the player which made me feel more like a mediator in other peoples affairs for each decision forced on me.

I didn't care about any character in the game, if they all had died it would not have affect the story or gameplay for me personally - in BG I & II however I did become attached to PCs in terms of their personal stories and what they added to my party (what is with the 4 person party size limit btw?). Jeheira's fight in and out of the Harpers or Jan's family issues or whatever were just more realistic that these stupid "I'm enslaved to a demon god, If I die the whole world will be destroyed" storylines that do not relate to a normal person.
